summary: Explains that URI structure is defined by its scheme and owner, and cautions against independent standards that mandate particular URI paths or structures on sites they do not own. It is best-practice guidance.

eli5.summary: Your street address belongs to your house. Outsiders should not decide how your rooms are named.

questions: can a specification mandate a url path
subtitle: Why standards should not dictate the shape of other people's URLs, and what to do instead.

tldr.problem: Specifications sometimes mandate fixed paths, query parameters or prefixes in URIs they do not own, which causes collisions and breaks deployments.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out rules per URI component: only the scheme definition, or the owner of the URI, decides structure. It points to links, URI Templates and well-known URIs as alternatives.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 7320 and updates RFC 3986, and turns many of the old hard rules into best-practice guidance.

today: RFC 8820 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 190) from June 2020. It obsoletes RFC 7320 and updates RFC 3986, and the metadata lists no later RFC replacing it.

sections.title: Why Outsiders Should Not Shape URIs
sections.content:
URIs often carry structured application data: filesystem artifacts in the path, user information in the query, sometimes even application data in the hostname. When the owner of the URI picks a server or application that imposes such structure, that is reasonable delegation. When a party other than the owner mandates it, the RFC lists five harms.

  • Collisions between ad hoc conventions.
  • Dilution, when ephemeral information in a URI reduces its stability.
  • Rigidity, for example a fixed base path such as /v1 that stops other applications sharing the prefix on a host.
  • Operational difficulty, such as a required query parameter that rules out servers serving files directly from a filesystem.
  • Client assumptions, such as a document saying the sig query parameter is a signature, so clients treat every sig that way.
sections.eli5: If a stranger decided that every house must have its front door painted blue, it would clash with the neighbours and annoy the people who live there. Owners should choose.

sections.title: Who the Guidance Is For
sections.content:
The guidance targets authors of specifications that constrain URI syntax or structure. Two classes are named. Extensions add capabilities that could apply to any identifier or a large subset, such as a new signature mechanism for http URIs. Applications use URIs for specific needs, such as an HTTP interface to particular information on a host. Requirements for Specifications apply to both.

The RFC does not stop legitimate owners from allocating control of their own URIs. A specification could define the meaning of a URI on IANA's web site when setting up a registry. Existing specifications that already deviate are left to the relevant communities to resolve, by updating the scheme definition or changing the specification.
sections.eli5: The rules are for people who write the rulebooks, not for people who live in the houses.

sections.title: Schemes and Authorities
sections.content:
Applications and Extensions can require specific URI schemes, for example both http and https. But Applications ought not preclude other schemes in the future unless they only work with the named ones. Substructure for schemes overall, such as a prefix or suffix on scheme names, MUST be done by modifying BCP 35, which the RFC calls an exceptional circumstance.

Scheme definitions set the format and meaning of the authority component. Other specifications MUST NOT constrain or define its structure or semantics, unless they update the scheme registration or the structures it relies on, such as DNS name syntax. An Extension cannot say that the foo prefix in https://foo_app.example.com is meaningful. Applications can nominate or constrain the port they use, when applicable.
sections.eli5: Only the post office can say how a postal address is written. A game rulebook cannot decide that every address starts with a magic word.

sections.title: Paths
sections.content:
Specifications MUST NOT define a fixed prefix for their URI paths, such as /myapp, unless the scheme definition allows it. The exception named is registered well-known URIs under RFC 8615.

This does not stop an Application from defining structure "under" a resource the server controls. Since the deployer controls that prefix, collisions and rigidity are avoided. For example an Application might define app_root as a deployment-controlled prefix, with resources at {app_root}/foo and {app_root}/bar. Extensions MUST NOT define structure within individual URI components, for example a prefix or suffix.
sections.eli5: You can tell people to look inside the box you hand them, but you cannot say that everyone's box has to sit on the same shelf.

sections.title: Queries and Fragment Identifiers
sections.content:
Applications can specify query syntax for resources under their control, though this can cause trouble for deployments that cannot support it, such as a site serving static files. Extensions MUST NOT constrain the format or meaning of queries. The RFC notes that HTML constrains query strings in form submission, and encourages new form languages to allow a broader variety of URIs, for example by creating new path components.

The syntax and semantics of fragment identifiers depend on the media type of the retrieved resource, per Section 3.5 of RFC 3986. Other specifications MUST NOT define structure within the fragment identifier, unless they define one for reuse by media types, as JSON Pointer (RFC 6901) does.
sections.eli5: What a note inside an envelope means depends on the kind of paper it is written on. An outsider cannot invent a new meaning for every note.

sections.title: Better Alternatives
sections.content:
The most successful approach is to use URIs as they were designed: as links exchanged within the protocol, not as statically specified syntax. The RFC names three tools.

  • Web Linking (RFC 8288) gives every link a relation type, context and target.
  • URI Templates (RFC 6570) insert application variables into a URI without impinging on the owner's control.
  • Well-known URIs (RFC 8615) reserve specific paths for standard use, but are not a general escape valve.

Elaborate structures to dodge collisions do not work. Prefixing query parameters with myapp_ still risks collision, because the prefix is not reserved.
sections.eli5: Instead of telling everyone where your room is, hand them a map with a clear arrow on it.
